power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 131 columns across 13 data files.
#### Issues Identified

16 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 13 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

#### File paths

**16 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `b1_data.rds` to `data/b1_data.rds` (in benchmark_helpers_V01.R); `b1_fit_lmer.rds` to `data/b1_fit_lmer.rds` (in benchmark_helpers_V01.R); `b2_fit_lavaan.rds` to `data/b2_fit_lavaan.rds` (in benchmark_helpers_V01.R); `b2_model.lav` to `data/b2_model.lav` (in benchmark_helpers_V01.R); `b3_data.rds` to `data/b3_data.rds` (in benchmark_helpers_V01.R); `b3_fit_mirt.rds` to `data/b3_fit_mirt.rds` (in benchmark_helpers_V01.R); `b4_data.rds` to `data/b4_data.rds` (in benchmark_helpers_V01.R); `b4_fit_lavaan_growth.rds` to `data/b4_fit_lavaan_growth.rds` (in benchmark_helpers_V01.R); `b4_model.lav` to `data/b4_model.lav` (in benchmark_helpers_V01.R); `b5_spec.txt` to `data/b5_spec.txt` (in benchmark_helpers_V01.R), and 6 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. The code reads files that are only inside `demo_rerun_060.zip`, `umg_0.6.0_source.zip`, `umg_0.6.0.zip`, `package/umg_0.6.0.tar.gz`, and no script unpacks them. We unpacked them in their folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks them (such as `unzip("demo_rerun_060.zip")` in R), or upload the files unpacked. **2 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.

The R package umg (version 0.6.0, the version executed for every result reported), the TikZ style library, the benchmark protocol with every script and rendering, the demonstration scripts with their output, and the sources of all figures are archived on the Open Science Framework at https://osf.io/d4xrm.
text.formatted: The R package umg (version 0.6.0, the version executed for every result reported), the TikZ style library, the benchmark protocol with every script and rendering, the demonstration scripts with their output, and the sources of all figures are archived on the Open Science Framework at <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/d4xrm">https://osf.io/d4xrm</ref>.

text.text: The illustrative analyses use openly available data sets named in the text.
No new data were collected.
This article is the reference publication for umg.
A related systematic review of diagramming practice is in preparation and shares no text with it.
The Unified Model Graph: Drawing the Statistical Models of Psychology Nearly every quantitative article in psychology includes a diagram of its statistical model.
Readers work from these figures.
A reviewer reconstructs the analysis from the figure before reading the tables.
A student learns a model from the figure before the equations.
Research on diagrammatic reasoning supports the habit: a good diagram carries some inferences better than the equivalent text (Larkin & Simon, 1987; Tversky, 2011).
text.formatted: Research on diagrammatic reasoning supports the habit: a good diagram carries some inferences better than the equivalent text <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Larkin & Simon, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Tversky, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: For latent variable, multilevel, mixture, and Bayesian models, the figure is often the main interface between the analyst and the reader.
The figure can only do this work if the reader can recover the model from it.
Often the reader cannot.
The diagramming conventions psychologists use grew up separately, each inside one modeling tradition.
Path diagrams came from structural equation modeling (Wright, 1921; Bollen, 1989).
text.formatted: Path diagrams came from structural equation modeling <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Wright, 1921;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bollen, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Panel schemes came from multilevel structural equation modeling (Mehta & Neale, 2005).
text.formatted: Panel schemes came from multilevel structural equation modeling <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Mehta & Neale, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Plate notation came from Bayesian modeling (Buntine, 1994; Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013).
text.formatted: Plate notation came from Bayesian modeling <ref type="bibr">(Buntine, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Causal graphs came from the causal inference literature (Pearl, 2009; Rohrer, 2018).
text.formatted: Causal graphs came from the causal inference literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Pearl, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Rohrer, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Network displays came from network psychometrics (Epskamp, Cramer, Waldorp, Schmittmann, & Borsboom, 2012; Borsboom & Cramer, 2013).
text.formatted: Network displays came from network psychometrics <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Epskamp, Cramer, Waldorp, Schmittmann, & Borsboom, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Borsboom & Cramer, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Each convention is coherent on its own.
Together they conflict on basic symbols.
A circle is a latent factor in one figure, any random quantity in another, and an observed variable in a third.
The models that mix traditions, which are now the common ones, inherit the conflicts.
The practical result is that one figure can stand for two different models.
An ellipse with arrows to three rectangles can show a one-factor model or a latent profile model.
A labeled arrow can show a fixed slope or a slope that varies across persons.
A mediation triangle can show a set of regressions or a set of causal claims.
In each case the two models have different implications, and the figure does not say which one the author fitted.
The reader must guess from the text, and the text does not always say.
This article proposes a fix in three parts.
The first part is a criterion.
A model diagram should be determinate: a reader who knows the notation should be able to recover, from the figure alone, the model that was fitted.
A determinate figure can be archived, compared with a preregistered version, checked for errors, and translated into estimation syntax.
An ambiguous figure cannot.
The second part is a notation that meets the criterion, the Unified Model Graph (UMG).
It types every quantity by three visual cues, types every dependence, marks replication with plates, and states its causal license on the figure.
The familiar conventions are special cases of it, so existing published figures translate rather than break.
The third part is software.
The R package umg builds, checks, translates, and renders UMG diagrams, and every figure and number in this article comes from archived scripts.
The claims are supported in three ways, and each claim is labeled by its kind of support.

Formal claims are proved: every well-formed UMG corresponds to exactly one family of observed-data distributions, the generalized latent variable models of psychology are covered, and the path diagram, plate notation, and causal graphs are recovered as special cases.
The proofs use standard graphical-model machinery (Lauritzen, 1996) and are given in the Supplemental Material that accompanies this article.
text.formatted: The proofs use standard graphical-model machinery <ref type="bibr">(Lauritzen, 1996)</ref> and are given in the Supplemental Material that accompanies this article.

text.text: Capability claims are demonstrated by execution: validation, round-trip translation with lavaan, identification checks, d-separation, model-implied displays, and diagram differencing all run in the archived scripts, and the numbers in this article are the numbers the scripts produce.
Comparative claims rest on an executed benchmark: eight R diagramming packages were tested on six models, ten representational features, and ten operations, with every script and rendering archived.
Claims about readers, for example that the notation is misread less often, are not tested here.
They are stated as hypotheses, and the Discussion describes the study that would test them.
The UMG is a notation with a semantics: a set of symbols, rules that say which figures are well formed, and a reading rule that maps every well-formed figure to a likelihood.
In the linguistic sense this makes it a grammar.
It is not a visualization grammar.
The grammar of graphics maps data to marks (Wilkinson, 2005; Wickham, 2010); this notation maps models to figures, and it renders through ordinary graphics backends.
text.formatted: The grammar of graphics maps data to marks <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Wilkinson, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Wickham, 2010)</ref>; this notation maps models to figures, and it renders through ordinary graphics backends.

text.text: The closest precedent is Curran and Bauer (2007), who extended path diagrams to random effects after showing that the classic convention could not draw them.
text.formatted: The closest precedent is <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Curran and Bauer (2007)</ref>, who extended path diagrams to random effects after showing that the classic convention could not draw them.

text.text: This article extends that move to the full model repertoire and adds the semantics and the software that make the figures checkable.
The path diagram is the oldest and most familiar convention.

It descends from Wright (1921 Wright ( , 1934)), entered the social sciences through path analysis (Duncan, 1966; Blau & Duncan, 1967), and matured with the confirmatory factor model (Jöreskog, 1969) and structural equation modeling (Bollen, 1989).
text.formatted: It descends from <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Wright (1921</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Wright ( , 1934))</ref>, entered the social sciences through path analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Duncan, 1966;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Blau & Duncan, 1967)</ref>, and matured with the confirmatory factor model <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Jöreskog, 1969)</ref> and structural equation modeling <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bollen, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: It draws observed variables as rectangles, latent variables as ellipses, directed effects as straight arrows, and covariances as curved double-headed arrows.
Its strongest feature was made explicit by the Reticular Action Model (McArdle & McDonald, 1984): for single-level linear models with continuous variables, the figure fixes the model exactly.
text.formatted: Its strongest feature was made explicit by the Reticular Action Model <ref type="bibr">(McArdle & McDonald, 1984)</ref>: for single-level linear models with continuous variables, the figure fixes the model exactly.

text.text: The directed edges fill one matrix, the covariance edges and variances fill a second, and the shading selects the observed variables.
Within that class, the diagram is a complete specification.
Outside that class, the convention runs out of symbols.

It has no symbol for a coefficient that varies across persons, so random effects are improvised with filled dots on arrows or arrows aimed at arrows; Curran and Bauer (2007) catalogued these improvisations.
text.formatted: It has no symbol for a coefficient that varies across persons, so random effects are improvised with filled dots on arrows or arrows aimed at arrows; <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Curran and Bauer (2007)</ref> catalogued these improvisations.

text.text: It has no symbol for a categorical latent variable, so a latent class cannot be drawn at all (Lazarsfeld & Henry, 1968; Goodman, 1974).
text.formatted: It has no symbol for a categorical latent variable, so a latent class cannot be drawn at all <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Lazarsfeld & Henry, 1968;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Goodman, 1974)</ref>.

text.text: It has no replication device, so multilevel structure is either absent from the figure or handled by splitting the diagram into within-level and between-level panels, which duplicates every variable that appears at both levels (Mehta & Neale, 2005).
text.formatted: It has no replication device, so multilevel structure is either absent from the figure or handled by splitting the diagram into within-level and between-level panels, which duplicates every variable that appears at both levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Mehta & Neale, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Plate notation solved the replication problem.
A rounded frame encloses the part of the model that repeats, nesting frames express hierarchy, and each vertex carries its distribution (Buntine, 1994; Gilks, Thomas, & Spiegelhalter, 1994).
text.formatted: A rounded frame encloses the part of the model that repeats, nesting frames express hierarchy, and each vertex carries its distribution <ref type="bibr">(Buntine, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Gilks, Thomas, & Spiegelhalter, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: The notation entered psychology with Bayesian modeling (Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013; Kruschke, 2015; McElreath, 2020).
text.formatted: The notation entered psychology with Bayesian modeling <ref type="bibr">(Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Kruschke, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">McElreath, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Its cost is that it types every unknown as a random variable.

It cannot separate a latent construct from a statistical parameter, a distinction psychologists treat as substantive (Borsboom, Mellenbergh, & van Heerden, 2003), and it has no curved edge for an unanalyzed covariance.
text.formatted: It cannot separate a latent construct from a statistical parameter, a distinction psychologists treat as substantive <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Borsboom, Mellenbergh, & van Heerden, 2003)</ref>, and it has no curved edge for an unanalyzed covariance.

text.text: The causal directed acyclic graph gave the arrow a sharper meaning: a claim that survives intervention.
Rules on the graph then determine what is identified from observational data (Pearl, 1995 (Pearl, , 2009)).
text.formatted: Rules on the graph then determine what is identified from observational data <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Pearl, 1995</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Pearl, , 2009))</ref>.

text.text: The framework entered psychology through the causal inference literature (Morgan & Winship, 2015; Rohrer, 2018), and it makes entire error classes visible on the figure, conditioning on a collider above all (Elwert & Winship, 2014).
text.formatted: The framework entered psychology through the causal inference literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Morgan & Winship, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Rohrer, 2018)</ref>, and it makes entire error classes visible on the figure, conditioning on a collider above all <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Elwert & Winship, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Its limitation for present purposes is narrow scope.
It carries no parameters, no distributions, and no replication device, and a causal graph looks the same on the page as a merely associational diagram with the same arrows.
Network psychometrics contributed the undirected edge.
Its figures display estimated conditional associations among observed variables (Epskamp et al., 2012; Borsboom & Cramer, 2013).
text.formatted: Its figures display estimated conditional associations among observed variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Epskamp et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Borsboom & Cramer, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These figures are pictures of estimates, not specifications of models, and a reader needs to know which of the two is on the page.
Table 1 summarizes the situation.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">1</ref> summarizes the situation.

text.text: Every convention captures something the others miss, and no convention covers the repertoire.
The conflicts appear exactly where current modeling lives: multilevel models with latent classes, measurement models inside causal designs, and Bayesian versions of all of them.
Table 1 lists  Table 1 Model Features Expressible in Each Diagramming Convention Note.

text.text: The right column shows the UMG device that separates them.
The model pairs are stated precisely in Part B of the Supplemental Material.
Panel (a) is the ellipse.
An ellipse labeled η i with arrows to three rectangles can show a one-factor model, in which η i is continuous.
It can equally show a latent profile model, in which η i takes one of K values (Lazarsfeld & Henry, 1968; Muthén & Shedden, 1999).

text.text: The two models differ in their implications.
The factor model implies a covariance matrix of rank one plus a diagonal.
The profile model implies a finite mixture of normals.
The figure does not choose between them, because the convention has no symbol for support. (a)

text.text: Under the second model, the conditional variance of y grows with x 2 ; under the first, it does not.
The figures coincide because the convention has no symbol for role or replication.
Panel (c) is the mediation triangle.
The three arrows can show a decomposition of the joint distribution into three regressions.
They can equally show a set of claims about what would happen under intervention.
Setting M by intervention is not the same as conditioning on M , so the two readings support different conclusions from the same estimates (Pearl, 1995; Rohrer, 2018).
text.formatted: Setting M by intervention is not the same as conditioning on M , so the two readings support different conclusions from the same estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Pearl, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Rohrer, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The figure does not say which reading the author intends.
A documented failure mode follows: the model that gets estimated matches the first reading, and the text narrates the second (Rohrer, 2018).
text.formatted: A documented failure mode follows: the model that gets estimated matches the first reading, and the text narrates the second <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Rohrer, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Panel (d) is plate notation.
A circle labeled µ outside the plate can show a fixed unknown estimated by maximum likelihood.
It can equally show a random variable whose prior the figure omits.
The two models differ: under the first, the observations are independent; under the second, they are marginally dependent.
Conventions that draw every random quantity as a circle separate the two cases only with a text annotation, and published figures often drop it.
These are not drawing errors.

Each convention was completed before the models it now has to carry existed, and each failure lands on models psychologists fit routinely: mixed-effects models, mixture and latent class models, item response models, and their Bayesian forms.

Reviews of reporting practice have documented for two decades that structural equation models are reported incompletely (McDonald & Ho, 2002; Jackson, Gillaspy, & Purc-Stephenson, 2009), and an audit of causal diagrams in applied health research found most published graphs incomplete relative to the text (Tennant et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Reviews of reporting practice have documented for two decades that structural equation models are reported incompletely <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(McDonald & Ho, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Jackson, Gillaspy, & Purc-Stephenson, 2009)</ref>, and an audit of causal diagrams in applied health research found most published graphs incomplete relative to the text <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Tennant et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: How often psychology's figures commit these four specific failures is an empirical question for a separate audit.
The present point is that the conventions permit the failures by construction.
Conventions spread through software defaults more than through style guides.
So the question of what the notations determine leads to a question about tools.
Eight R packages that draw statistical model diagrams were benchmarked on six models chosen to exercise the features in Table 1.
text.formatted: Eight R packages that draw statistical model diagrams were benchmarked on six models chosen to exercise the features in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: The six models were: a regression with a person-varying slope; the three-factor model of the Holzinger and Swineford data; a crossed two-parameter item response model; a two-class growth mixture model; a Bayesian two-parameter item response model; and a mediation model with a latent confounder, read once associationally and once causally.

The packages were semPlot (Epskamp, 2015), lavaanPlot (Lishinski, 2024), tidySEM (van Lissa, 2026), ggsem (Min, 2026), umx (T. C. Bates, Maes, & Neale, 2019), ggdag (Barrett, 2024), dagitty (Textor, van der Zander, Gilthorpe, Liśkiewicz, & Ellison, 2016), and DiagrammeR (Iannone & Roy, 2026) as the generic Graphviz baseline.

Protocol, scripts, and renderings: the benchmark materials in the OSF repository.
The notation rests on a typology of the quantities a statistical model mentions.

Any such quantity, a test score, a latent trait, a factor loading, a class membership, a design constant, can be classified by its answers to three questions, and the three answers are logically independent of one another.
The existing conventions collapse these questions into fewer symbols than the answers require, and that collapse is where their ambiguities begin.
The UMG assigns each question its own visual channel, so every combination of answers has its own appearance on the page.
The first question concerns observability: is the quantity recorded in the data, or is it inferred from the data through the model?
An item response is recorded; the ability assumed to underlie it is inferred.

The distinction matters because observed and latent quantities play different roles in estimation and in validity arguments, and because a reader must be able to see which parts of a figure the data constrain directly.
The UMG encodes observability with fill: observed quantities are shaded, latent quantities are open.
The second question concerns support: does the quantity take values on a continuum, or in a finite set of categories?
A factor score and a reaction time are continuous; a latent class and a binary response are categorical.
Support determines the mathematical form of every distribution attached to the quantity, and, for latent variables, it is the difference between a factor model and a mixture model.
The UMG encodes support with shape: circles for continuous quantities, squares for categorical ones.
The third question concerns inferential role: how does the quantity enter the likelihood?
Four roles cover the models in scope.
A random variable carries a probability distribution.
A parameter is a fixed unknown that estimation targets.
A deterministic quantity is an exact function of other quantities, such as a sum score.
A constant is a value fixed by design, such as the unit constant that carries a mean.

The UMG encodes role with the outline: a single border for a random variable, an open diamond for a parameter, a double border for a deterministic quantity, and a triangle for a constant, the last inherited from the Reticular Action Model (McArdle & McDonald, 1984).
text.formatted: The UMG encodes role with the outline: a single border for a random variable, an open diamond for a parameter, a double border for a deterministic quantity, and a triangle for a constant, the last inherited from the Reticular Action Model <ref type="bibr">(McArdle & McDonald, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: The independence of the three questions is the point of the typology.
Observability does not determine support: a latent variable may be continuous, as a factor is, or categorical, as a class is.
Role does not follow from the other two: on a frequentist reading a loading is a fixed unknown, and on a Bayesian reading the same loading is a random variable with a prior.

The classic structural equation lexicon offers a single contrast, rectangle versus ellipse, and that one contrast suffices only where observability, support, and role happen to move together, which they do in single-level linear models with continuous variables and nowhere else in the modern repertoire.
Separating the three questions is what lets the notation reach that repertoire.

It also generates symbols rather than stipulating them: a latent class is latent, categorical, and random, so it is drawn as an open square with a single border, an object no older convention possesses and this notation did not have to invent.
Figure 2 displays the complete lexicon, and Table 4 states which visual channel carries which meaning.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref> displays the complete lexicon, and Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">4</ref> states which visual channel carries which meaning.

text.text: The channel assignments follow the graphical perception literature.
Value and shape suit nominal distinctions such as observed versus latent (Bertin, 1983), and the magnitude The UMG Lexicon (a)  that repeats, labeled by its index.
text.formatted: Value and shape suit nominal distinctions such as observed versus latent <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bertin, 1983)</ref>, and the magnitude The UMG Lexicon (a)  that repeats, labeled by its index.

text.text: A measurement model drawn once inside a person plate repeats independently for every person.
Nested plates express hierarchy, such as occasions within persons.
Overlapping plates express crossing, such as persons by items.
The plate states the exchangeability assumption that justifies pooling.
The classic path diagram leaves that assumption to the reader.
A small badge in the corner states whether the figure makes a causal claim.
Under the statistical badge, the arrows describe only how the joint distribution factors.
Under the structural badge, the directed edges among substantive quantities are asserted to be stable under intervention, which makes the figure a causal model in the sense of Pearl (1995).
text.formatted: Under the structural badge, the directed edges among substantive quantities are asserted to be stable under intervention, which makes the figure a causal model in the sense of <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Pearl (1995)</ref>.

text.text: A notation must also say which figures are not allowed.
Some arrangements of the symbols above look like models but describe none, and if such figures were permitted, no
Following the directed edges, stochastic, deterministic, or mixing, must never lead from a vertex back to itself.
A directed cycle would leave no order in which the model could generate its quantities, so no factorization of the joint distribution would exist.
Every vertex with no incoming edge must be able to start the generative account.

Four kinds of vertex can: a parameter, a constant, an observed random vertex annotated as conditioned on (the familiar fixed-regressor convention), and a random vertex that carries its own unconditional distribution.
A bare random vertex with no distribution and no parents gives the model no way to generate it, and the package warns about it.
A covariance edge may join only two random vertices that both carry Gaussian annotations, and it then declares one free covariance between their disturbances.
This blocks meaningless associations, such as a covariance between a parameter and a constant, which would assert an association between quantities that do not vary jointly.
One further clause keeps the generative order intact: merge every covariance-connected group of vertices into a single vertex, and the directed graph that remains must still be acyclic.
A mixing edge must start at a latent categorical random vertex and must point at a parameter or a distribution annotation, never at an observed vertex.
The rule encodes what a mixture is: class membership switches the regime that generates the data, so it acts on parameters, not on a data point directly.
An edge from a continuous latent vertex, or from an observed grouping variable, is not mixing and is refused; an observed grouping variable enters as an ordinary predictor instead.
Plates must fit together, and edges must respect them.
Three clauses say how.
First, any two plates must be disjoint, nested, or explicitly declared crossed, the nesting must not cycle, and a vertex inside a nested plate belongs to every enclosing plate.
Second, a covariance edge may join only vertices with the same plate membership, because a covariance between quantities replicated over different index sets is not defined.
Third, a directed edge is licensed only when every plate containing its source also contains its target; otherwise one copy of the target would have to depend on many copies of the source.

This is the clause that keeps crossed designs honest: an item parameter, which exists once per item, may point at a response, which exists once per person and item, but not at an ability, which exists once per person.
A deterministic aggregate declared as such, a cluster mean for example, is the licensed exception.
A mixing edge follows the same logic: every random vertex whose distribution the selected parameter governs must lie inside the plates of the class vertex.
Every part of the figure must carry the information the reading rule needs.
Every random vertex carries a distribution, or is an observed source annotated as conditioned on, and every deterministic vertex carries its defining function.

Structural equation diagrams may leave the routine annotations implicit; the linear-Gaussian default of that tradition then fills them in, a linear equation in the vertex's parents with a free Gaussian disturbance.
This condition makes the reading rule total: it never meets a vertex it cannot read.
Together the six conditions do for the notation what a syntax does for a programming language.

They separate the figures that specify a model from the figures that merely resemble one, they localize each failure to a nameable condition, and they make refusal automatic: the package checks all six on construction and reports the violated condition in its error message, as the validation demonstration below shows.
A well-formed UMG can be read as a likelihood, and the reading is mechanical.
Each random vertex contributes a conditional density given its parents.
Vertices joined by covariance edges contribute one joint Gaussian block.
Plates multiply these contributions over their indices.
Mixing edges substitute the parameter copy that the class membership selects.
The product of all contributions is the joint distribution of everything the model mentions.
Integrating out the continuous latent quantities and summing out the categorical ones gives the likelihood of the observed data.
The sum over latent categories is exactly the finite mixture that defines latent class and mixture models (McLachlan & Peel, 2000; Muthén & Shedden, 1999).
text.formatted: The sum over latent categories is exactly the finite mixture that defines latent class and mixture models <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(McLachlan & Peel, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Muthén & Shedden, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: This construction is the standard one for graphical models (Pearl, 1988; Lauritzen, Dawid, Larsen, & Leimer, 1990; Lauritzen, 1996).
text.formatted: This construction is the standard one for graphical models <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Pearl, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lauritzen, Dawid, Larsen, & Leimer, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lauritzen, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: What is new is the guarantee that it applies to every well-formed figure in this notation.
Two formal results back the guarantee, and both are stated and proved in Part B of the Supplemental Material.
The first is soundness and determinacy.

For every well-formed UMG, the construction above yields a valid likelihood, the result does not depend on the order in which the figure is read, and the figure corresponds to exactly one family of observed-data distributions.
In short, the diagram is not a picture of the model.
It is the model, drawn.
The second result is coverage.
Every model built from parametric conditionals, Gaussian covariance blocks, nested or crossed replication, and finite mixing over categorical latent variables has a well-formed UMG.

This class includes confirmatory and exploratory factor models, linear and generalized structural equation models, the standard item response families, generalized linear mixed and latent growth models, latent class, latent profile, and growth mixture models, diagnostic classification models, and the
Bayesian extension of any of them.
The examples in this article illustrate the coverage result; they do not substitute for it.
Where coverage ends, at continuous-time dynamics, at nonparametric Bayesian structures, and at estimated networks, the boundary is stated in the Discussion.
Three further results, also proved in Part B of the Supplemental Material, show that the older conventions are special cases.

Restrict the notation to one person plate, continuous variables, linear-Gaussian annotations, and the statistical badge, and it reduces to the recursive path diagram of the Reticular Action Model (McArdle & McDonald, 1984; Bollen, 1989).

text.text: Restrict it to diagrams without covariance edges in which every parameter has a prior, and it reduces to plate notation (Buntine, 1994; Koller & Friedman, 2009).

text.text: Under the structural badge, replace each covariance edge with a latent common cause, and the directed edges among substantive vertices form a causal directed acyclic graph to which the do-calculus applies (Pearl, 2009).

text.text: The path diagram and the plate diagram turn out to be the same notation specialized in two directions.
Each kept the distinctions the other dropped.
That is why the two were never reconcilable on their own terms, and why one notation can contain both.
The most useful single idea in the notation starts from the simplest model psychologists fit.
Figure 3, panel (a), is an ordinary regression.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>, panel (a), is an ordinary regression.

text.text: The predictor and outcome are shaded circles inside a person plate.
The coefficient β, which the path tradition writes as a label on the arrow, is drawn as a diamond outside the plate, feeding the arrow it would have labeled.
Nothing about the model has changed.
The label has become an object.
Now relocate the diamond.
Move it inside the plate and give it a distribution across persons, and the fixed coefficient becomes a random effect (panel b).
This is the multilevel move that path-diagram syntax cannot draw, done by moving one vertex (Curran & Bauer, 2007; Mehta & Neale, 2005).
text.formatted: This is the multilevel move that path-diagram syntax cannot draw, done by moving one vertex <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Curran & Bauer, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Mehta & Neale, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Give the parameter a prior instead, and it becomes the latent quantity of a Bayesian model; the diamond turns into an open circle whose parents are the constants of the prior (panel c).
Point a mixing edge from a latent class vertex at it, and the single coefficient becomes a set of class-specific coefficients; the model is now a mixture (panel d).
A fixed effect, a random effect, a Bayesian prior, and a class-specific parameter are one graphical object in four positions.
The statistical content of this observation is not new.
Random effects are latent variables, a prior turns a parameter into a random variable, and a mixture switches parameters with a latent class.

These are the unifying insights of generalized latent variable modeling (Muthén, 2002; Rabe-Hesketh, Skrondal, & Pickles, 2004; Skrondal & Rabe-Hesketh, 2004) and hierarchical Bayesian practice (Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013; Kruschke, 2015).
text.formatted: These are the unifying insights of generalized latent variable modeling <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Muthén, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Rabe-Hesketh, Skrondal, & Pickles, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Skrondal & Rabe-Hesketh, 2004</ref>) and hierarchical Bayesian practice <ref type="bibr">(Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Kruschke, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: What is new is graphical.
The four positions look different on the page, the move between them is one relocation, and the compound figures compose.
The payoff can be computed.

A notation spreads through software, so the notation comes with software.
This section describes the package's concept, design, and functions.
Part A of the Supplemental Material complements it with installation instructions and a complete worked example; the two are meant to be read together.
The central design decision is that the diagram itself is the object the software manipulates.

The R package umg (Yu, 2026) represents a UMG as a typed data structure that carries everything the notation defines: the vertices with their observability, support, and role; the typed edges; the plates with their nesting and crossing declarations; the distribution annotations; and the badge.
text.formatted: The R package umg <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Yu, 2026)</ref> represents a UMG as a typed data structure that carries everything the notation defines: the vertices with their observability, support, and role; the typed edges; the plates with their nesting and crossing declarations; the distribution annotations; and the badge.

text.text: Every operation in the package reads or writes this one structure.
Because the structure carries the full typing, the well-formedness conditions become mechanical checks, and the package runs them on construction.
A directed cycle is refused (W1).
A covariance edge that joins non-random vertices is refused (the first clause of W3).
A mixing edge with an ill-typed source or target is refused (W4).
An edge or plate declaration that breaks the plate rules is refused (all clauses of W5, including index licensing).
A source vertex without a distribution draws a warning (W2), and the linear-Gaussian defaults are supplied where W6 permits them.
A figure that does not denote a model is never drawn.
The functions form four groups.

Construction functions build the object: the constructors umg_node(), umg_edge(), umg_plate(), and umg_model() assemble a diagram element by element, and one-line builders such as umg_factor(), umg_growth(), umg_mixture(), and umg_riclpm() return ready diagrams for the common families.

Translation functions connect the object to estimation software: umg_from_lavaan(), umg_from_lmer(), and their counterparts for mirt, brms, blavaan, OpenMx, and qgraph build a diagram from a fitted object (Rosseel, 2012; D. Bates, Mächler, Bolker, & Walker, 2015; Chalmers, 2012; Neale et al., 2016; Epskamp et al., 2012), and umg_to_lavaan() emits estimation syntax from a diagram.
text.formatted: Translation functions connect the object to estimation software: umg_from_lavaan(), umg_from_lmer(), and their counterparts for mirt, brms, blavaan, OpenMx, and qgraph build a diagram from a fitted object <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Rosseel, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">D. Bates, Mächler, Bolker, & Walker, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chalmers, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Neale et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Epskamp et al., 2012)</ref>, and umg_to_lavaan() emits estimation syntax from a diagram.

text.text: Interrogation functions read the object: umg_validate() checks well-formedness; umg_identify(), with umg_check_scaling(), umg_count_parameters(), and umg_labelswitching(), runs the identification readings; umg_dsep() and umg_implied_ci() derive testable implications; and umg_eda_scaffold() and umg_caterpillar() generate the model-implied data displays.
Rendering functions draw it: the same object renders through four backends, grid, ggplot2, Graphviz, and TikZ, and umg_save() writes any of them to file.
Every figure in this article was produced with the TikZ library that accompanies the package.
Because a well-formed UMG fixes the likelihood, the figure is a formal object, and software can operate on it.
This section demonstrates six operations.
Every demonstration is an archived script with its output, and the numbers quoted here are the numbers the scripts produce.
The well-formedness conditions are checked on construction .
A three-vertex directed cycle is refused with the message "W1 violated: directed subgraph (dep/det/mix) contains a cycle."
A mixing edge whose source is a continuous latent vertex named eta is refused with "W4 violated: mix edge source 'eta' is not a latent categorical random vertex."
A mixing edge aimed directly at an observed vertex y is refused with "W4 violated: mix edge targets observed vertex 'y' directly."
A covariance edge joining a latent vertex to a parameter lambda is refused with "W3 violated: cov edge eta <-> lambda joins non-random vertices."
text.formatted: A covariance edge joining a latent vertex to a parameter lambda is refused with "W3 violated: cov edge eta <-> lambda joins non-random vertices."

text.text: An edge that the plate structure cannot carry is also refused: aiming an item-plate parameter a at a person-plate ability theta produces "W5 violated: edge a -> theta is not licensed by the index structure (plates of 'a' are not contained in the plates of 'theta')."
text.formatted: An edge that the plate structure cannot carry is also refused: aiming an item-plate parameter a at a person-plate ability theta produces "W5 violated: edge a -> theta is not licensed by the index structure (plates of 'a' are not contained in the plates of 'theta')."

text.text: The well-formed counterpart of each refused figure, for example a latent class vertex selecting a parameter that feeds the observed vertex, is accepted.
In the benchmark, no other package refused the cyclic specification, and every package that accepted it drew it.
A determinate figure can be translated into estimation syntax and back.
For a covariance structure, the round trip is exact.
Figure 4 shows the operation on the three-factor model of the Holzinger and Swineford data (Holzinger & Swineford, 1939; Rosseel, 2012).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">4</ref> shows the operation on the three-factor model of the Holzinger and Swineford data <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Holzinger & Swineford, 1939;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rosseel, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The model is fitted in lavaan.

The diagram is built from the fitted object. fit <-cfa("visual =~x1 + x2 + x3 textual =~x4 + x5 + x6 speed =~x7 + x8 + x9", data = HolzingerSwineford1939) m <-umg_from_lavaan(fit) # fitted object -> diagram umg_validate(m) # W1 to W6: TRUE cat(umg_to_lavaan(m)) # diagram -> syntax refit <-cfa(umg_to_lavaan(m), data = HolzingerSwineford1939) ## original refit |difference| ## npar 21.000 21.000 0 ## df 24.000 24.000 0 ## chisq 85.306 85.306 0 ## cfi 0.931 0.931 0 ## rmsea 0.092 0.092 0 ## srmr 0.065 0.065 0 ## max |estimate difference| over 24 matched parameters: 2.2e-16

text.text: Note.
Output abridged from the archived script demo_roundtrip_V01.

The diagram built from the fitted object has 12 vertices (9 observed, 3 latent), 9 stochastic edges with the marker loadings fixed at 1, 3 covariance edges, and one person plate. lavaan syntax is emitted from the diagram, and the emitted syntax is refitted.

The two fits are identical: 21 free parameters, 24 degrees of freedom, χ 2 (24) = 85.31, CFI = .931, RMSEA = .092, SRMR = .065 in both, with a maximum absolute difference in parameter estimates of 2.2 × 10 -16 across the 24 matched parameters.
The same round trip on a linear latent growth model is also exact.

The emitted syntax includes the intercept and mean rows, and refitting it with lavaan's growth function reproduces the original fit: 9 free parameters, 5 degrees of freedom, and a maximum absolute difference in estimates of 2.3 × 10 -15 .
Translation from the figure is what a preregistration needs.
The benchmark found syntax emission in four of the eight packages, in each case from the package's own model object rather than from a typed diagram.
Because the figure fixes the likelihood, necessary conditions of identification can be read from it before estimation.
Three readings are implemented.
The scaling check inspects every latent continuous vertex for a unit loading or a fixed variance; a constant parent is reported separately as fixing location, not scale.
A one-factor diagram without a scaling mark is reported as unscaled.
The same diagram with a marker loading or a unit variance passes.
The counting rule compares the free quantities in the figure with the distinct covariance moments of the observed vertices.
This is the graphical form of the t-rule (Bollen, 1989).
text.formatted: This is the graphical form of the t-rule <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bollen, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: The Holzinger and Swineford diagram returns 45 moments, 21 free parameters, and 24 degrees of freedom, matching the fitted model.
A two-indicator factor returns -1 and is flagged as under-identified.
The four-wave random-intercept cross-lagged panel diagram returns 36 moments, 27 free parameters, and 9 degrees of freedom, the published count (Hamaker et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The four-wave random-intercept cross-lagged panel diagram returns 36 moments, 27 free parameters, and 9 degrees of freedom, the published count <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hamaker et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: With its mean-structure option, the counting rule on the growth diagram returns 14 moments, 9 free parameters, and 5 degrees of freedom, matching lavaan's growth function.
The label-switching check reports, for any diagram with a latent class vertex, that the model is identified only up to permutation of the class labels (Bauer, 2007).
text.formatted: The label-switching check reports, for any diagram with a latent class vertex, that the model is identified only up to permutation of the class labels <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bauer, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: On the growth mixture diagram it names the class vertex, and the counting rule declares itself inapplicable with a warning, because covariance moments are not a valid check for a mixture.
All three readings are necessary conditions only, and they apply to single-level covariance structures.
No graphical reading replaces a formal identification analysis.
What each reading does is catch a routine error at the drawing board, where it is cheapest to fix.

Because a diagram without covariance edges reduces to plate notation, the directed Markov property applies, and the conditional independencies a diagram implies can be read off it by d-separation, with covariance edges treated as latent common causes (Lauritzen et al., 1990).

text.text: On the mediation diagram of Figure 9 with a direct path, X and Y are reported dependent given M and marginally.
text.formatted: On the mediation diagram of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_22">9</ref> with a direct path, X and Y are reported dependent given M and marginally.

text.text: With the direct path removed, they are reported independent given M .

With the direct path restored and a latent confounder of M and Y added, X and Y remain dependent given M ; X and the confounder are marginally independent; and conditioning on M makes them dependent, because M is a collider on the path between them.

The back-door path from M to Y through the confounder cannot be blocked by observed variables, so neither the effect of M on Y nor the direct effect of X adjusted for M is identified while the confounder is unmeasured (Pearl, 1995).

A dependence edge between continuous quantities implies the scatterplot that would expose a nonlinear relation behind a linear coefficient.

A random-coefficient vertex implies the spaghetti plot of person-specific trajectories.

text.text: A determinate figure can be differenced.
The package exposes a diagram's vertices and edges as data frames, so a preregistered diagram and its estimated successor can be compared with ordinary set operations.

For the Holzinger and Swineford model, comparing the preregistered three-factor diagram with a final diagram in which the ninth test also loads on the visual factor returns exactly one added edge, no removed edges, and an identical vertex set.
The counting rule reports the change from 24 to 23 degrees of freedom.
Revising a model during analysis is not the problem the replication literature identified.
Reporting the revised model as if it had been planned is (Wagenmakers et al., 2012).

text.text: A figure that can be versioned and diffed like a script makes the revision visible.
The case for the notation is made by drawing the models psychologists fit.

Each uses a feature the path diagram lacks, and each connects to one of the operations above.
Every figure was drawn with the TikZ library that accompanies the package.

text.text: Item response models break the classic convention immediately.
The responses are categorical.
The item parameters are neither latent constructs nor observed data; they are fixed unknowns.
Persons and items are crossed, not nested, because every person answers every item (Lord & Novick, 1968; Embretson & Reise, 2000).

text.text: Under the statistical badge, the arrows license only a decomposition of the joint distribution into regressions.
That is the reading the data alone support.
Under the structural badge, the same topology gains a latent confounder of the mediator and the outcome, and the causal reading becomes available and disciplined.

The d-separation reading demonstrated above, applied to the structural panel, shows that the back-door path from the mediator to the outcome cannot be blocked by observed variables, and that conditioning on the mediator opens a collider path from the exposure to the confounder.
Neither the mediator's effect nor the direct effect adjusted for the mediator is identified unless the confounder is measured (Pearl, 1995; Rohrer, 2018).

The argument of this article is short.
A model diagram should let the reader recover the model that was fitted.
The conventions psychology uses do not, for the models psychologists now fit most.
A notation that types quantities on three dimensions, types dependencies, marks replication, and states its license does, and the guarantee is proved Three limits bound the claims.
The first is scope.
The coverage result includes the directed, finitely mixed, parametric models that dominate current practice.

It stops short of continuous-time and dynamic structural equation models, of nonparametric Bayesian structures whose dimension is itself unknown, and of estimated networks, which the notation can display but not fully specify because they are pictures of fitted quantities (Borsboom & Cramer, 2013).
text.formatted: It stops short of continuous-time and dynamic structural equation models, of nonparametric Bayesian structures whose dimension is itself unknown, and of estimated networks, which the notation can display but not fully specify because they are pictures of fitted quantities <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Borsboom & Cramer, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Extending the plate machinery to random and growing index sets is the next formal problem.
The second limit is the implementation.
Version 0.6.0 of umg is the version executed for every result here, and it has three known gaps.
It stores distribution annotations but does not print them through its automatic renderers, and it leaves residual variances implicit in rendered figures.
Its counting and scaling readings apply to single-level covariance structures.
In the MIMIC and formative motifs, it treats the observed causes as modeled rather than conditioned on, so their free covariances are omitted from the count.
Each gap is recorded in the archived materials with reproduction code.
None of the formal results depends on the implementation.
The third limit concerns readers, and it is the one the notation now makes testable.

The channel allocation follows the graphical perception literature (Cleveland & McGill, 1984), but no experiment here shows that UMG figures are read faster or misread less often than conventional figures.

text.text: The natural study is a preregistered within-subjects comparison.
Graduate students and reviewers see figures in conventional notation and in the UMG.

They identify which quantities are latent, which effects vary across persons, how many latent classes the model posits, whether a causal reading is licensed, and how many free parameters the model has.
Accuracy and response time are scored and analyzed with crossed random effects for participants and items.
The exhibits of Figure 1 supply the stimuli on which the notations should differ most, and the materials of this article supply the figures.
text.formatted: The exhibits of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref> supply the stimuli on which the notations should differ most, and the materials of this article supply the figures.

text.text: Until that study is run, the perceptual and pedagogical benefits of the notation are hypotheses with a design attached.
Two consequences for practice do not wait on that study.
First, determinacy can be demanded of a figure in any notation.

Typed quantities, typed dependencies, explicit replication, and a declared license can be achieved in a classic path diagram through disciplined use of its own devices plus a caption that states the rest.

Reporting standards already ask for completeness in model reporting (Appelbaum et al., 2018; McDonald & Ho, 2002); determinacy gives the figure-level version of that demand, and an audit of how often published figures meet it is the natural companion study.

The package imports only base R packages (grid, grDevices, stats, tools, utils).
The converters and the ggplot2 backend use suggested packages (lavaan, lme4, mirt, brms, blavaan, OpenMx, qgraph, ggplot2) only when called.
A diagram is built from three constructors: umg_node() for vertices, umg_edge() for edges, and umg_plate() for plates. umg_model() assembles them and validates on construction.

The example below is the two-indicator factor diagram from the archived validation script. library(umg) m <-umg_model( nodes = list( umg_node("eta", "$\\eta_i$", observed = FALSE, dist = "N(0, psi)"), umg_node("y1", "$y_{1i}$", observed = TRUE), umg_node("y2", "$y_{2i}$", observed = TRUE) ), edges = list( umg_edge("eta", "y1", "dep", fixed = 1), umg_edge("eta", "y2", "dep", label = "$\\lambda_2$") ), plates = list(umg_plate("person", c("eta", "y1", "y2"), "i = 1, ..., N")) ) umg_validate(m) # TRUE

This part states the formal results the article relies on and proves them.
The machinery is that of directed graphical models (Lauritzen, Dawid, Larsen, & Leimer, 1990; Lauritzen, 1996).
text.formatted: The machinery is that of directed graphical models <ref type="bibr">(Lauritzen, Dawid, Larsen, & Leimer, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lauritzen, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: The reading equations come first, then the definitions, then the results with their proofs.

types each vertex by observability O = {obs, lat}, support S = {cont, cat}, and role R = {rv, par, det, const}; Π is a finite set of plates, each a pair (S p , I p ) of a scope S p ⊆ V and a finite index set I p ; and α assigns a conditional density (with respect to a fixed σ-finite measure on the vertex's support) to each vertex of role rv, given its parents, and a measurable function of its parents to each vertex of role det.

A vertex of role par that is the target of a mix edge from a categorical vertex c with K values denotes a K-vector θ (1) , . . . , θ (K) ; wherever that parameter enters a density, the value θ (c) is substituted, so that c is a parent of every random vertex whose density involves the parameter.

A parameter targeted by mix edges from several categorical vertices denotes an array indexed by the product of their value sets, and a mix edge into a distribution annotation is read the same way, with the annotation's parameters treated as an implicit parameter vertex.
For v ∈ V write plates(v) = {p ∈ Π : v ∈ S p } and pa(v) for the set of tails of dep and det edges into v together with the sources of mix edges whose targets enter the density of v.
The badge is a flag in {statistical, structural}.
Definition 2 (Well-formedness).

G is well-formed when W1 to W6 of the main text hold, with W3 including the condition that the graph obtained by merging each set of covariance-linked vertices into one vertex is acyclic, with W6 exempting observed sources annotated as conditioned on, and with W5 read as: (W5a) for any two plates, S p ∩ S q = ∅, or S p ⊆ S q , or S q ⊆ S p , or the pair is declared crossed, and the inclusion relation is acyclic; (W5b) a vertex in a plate nested in q is in S q ; (W5c) for every edge (u, v, k) with k = dep, plates(u) ⊆ plates(v); for k = det the same holds unless v is annotated as an aggregate over plates(u) \ plates(v); for k = cov, plates(u) = plates(v); and for k = mix with source c, plates(c) ⊆ plates(w) for every random vertex w whose density involves the target.
Definition 3 (Instantiation).

The instantiation of G is the graph G * whose vertices are the pairs (v, ι) with v ∈ V and ι a tuple of indices, one from I p for each p ∈ plates(v), and whose edges join (u, ι u ) to (v, ι v ) whenever u ∈ pa(v) and ι u is the restriction of ι v to plates(u); for a deterministic aggregate v, the parents of (v, ι v ) are all (u, ι u ) whose restriction to plates(v) equals ι v .
A mix-targeted parameter vertex is instantiated over its own plates as usual; the copy (c, ι c ) of its source selects which of its K values enters each density that involves it.
W5c is exactly the condition under which the restrictions in Definition 3 are defined, so every instantiated vertex has a well-defined set of instantiated parents, each appearing once.
Definition 4 (Induced family).

Let θ collect the values of the par vertices, the free edge labels, and the free quantities of the annotations (variances, covariances, link and mixing parameters), let Θ be the set of values for which every annotation is a density (positive definite covariance blocks, mixing proportions on the simplex), and fix the const vertices.
Observed source vertices annotated as conditioned on are held fixed throughout.
Equation 1 applied to G * defines p(V * rv ; θ); Equation 2 defines L(θ) as the marginal density of the observed instantiated vertices given the conditioned sources.
The induced family is {L(• ; θ) : θ ∈ Θ}.
Result 1 (Soundness and determinacy).
Let G be a well-formed UMG.

Then the righthand side of Equation 1 is a probability density for every value of the free quantities in the admissible parameter set, it does not depend on the order in which vertices, blocks, or plates are enumerated, and Equation 2 is well defined.
Consequently G determines exactly one family of observed-data distributions, indexed by its parameter vertices, free edge labels, and free annotation quantities.
Proof.
Let G be well-formed, G * its instantiation, and θ ∈ Θ. (i) The instantiated directed graph is acyclic: a directed cycle in G * projects onto a directed closed walk in G, which W1 forbids.

Let the instantiated random vertices be partitioned into blocks, each block a maximal set joined by cov edges; by W5c every cov edge joins vertices with identical plate membership, so blocks are well defined after instantiation.
The quotient graph over blocks is acyclic, because it is the instantiation of the merged graph that the second clause of W3 requires to be acyclic, and a cycle within one block is excluded by W1.
Choose a topological order of the blocks.

By W6 every random vertex carries a conditional density given its parents, and by W3 every block with more than one vertex is jointly Gaussian given its external parents, its internal directed edges absorbed into the block's reduced form, with a disturbance covariance matrix whose free off-diagonal elements are those marked by cov edges; for θ ∈ Θ that covariance is positive definite, so the block density is a valid conditional density.
By W2 every block without parents carries an unconditional density or is held fixed.

The product of conditional densities along a topological order is a joint density, since integrating the last factor over its own variables gives one and the argument repeats down the order (Lauritzen et al., 1990). (ii) The product over a finite index set is commutative, so the value does not depend on the topological order chosen or on the order in which plates are enumerated; and instantiation commutes with factorization because, by Definition 3, the parents of an instantiated vertex are determined by the edges of G and the index tuple alone. (iii) Marginalizing a joint density over a subset of its variables, by integration over continuous latent vertices and summation over categorical ones, yields a density of the remaining variables for every θ, so L(θ) is well defined.
text.formatted: The product of conditional densities along a topological order is a joint density, since integrating the last factor over its own variables gives one and the argument repeats down the order <ref type="bibr">(Lauritzen et al., 1990)</ref>. (ii) The product over a finite index set is commutative, so the value does not depend on the topological order chosen or on the order in which plates are enumerated; and instantiation commutes with factorization because, by Definition 3, the parents of an instantiated vertex are determined by the edges of G and the index tuple alone. (iii) Marginalizing a joint density over a subset of its variables, by integration over continuous latent vertices and summation over categorical ones, yields a density of the remaining variables for every θ, so L(θ) is well defined.

text.text: Finally, each step above is a function of (V, E, τ, Π, α) and θ; hence the map from well-formed diagrams to induced families is a function, and G determines exactly one family.
Result 1 concerns the map from the tuple (V, E, τ, Π, α) to the family.

The map from a drawn figure to the tuple is also a function, because each reserved visual channel of the lexicon (the channel table of the main article) encodes exactly one component of the typing and the W6 defaults are fixed; the composite map from figure to family is therefore a function, which is the sense in which the drawn figure is determinate.
Result 2 (Coverage).

Let M be the smallest class of models that contains every parametric conditional distribution whose parameters are smooth functions of a linear predictor in its parents, and that is closed under directed composition, jointly Gaussian blocks with structured covariance, independent and identically distributed replication over nested or crossed index sets conditional on the quantities not replicated, and finite mixing over a categorical latent variable.
Every model in M admits a well-formed UMG whose induced family under Equations 1 and 2 is the model.
Proof.
Define M inductively.
Base: a single random variable y with conditional density f (y | η) in a parametric family, where η = g(β ⊤ z) for parents z (possibly empty), a smooth link g, and parameters β.

Closure rules: (composition) the joint of two members over disjoint response sets whose union of parent relations is acyclic and whose index structures are compatible, in that a quantity shared by both carries the same plate membership in each; (Gaussian block) a set of responses jointly Gaussian given their external parents with covariance free on a specified set of off-diagonal positions; (replication) independent and identically distributed copies of a member over a finite index set, conditional on the quantities not replicated, with the index set nested in or crossed with existing index sets; (mixing) a member whose parameter subvector θ S is replaced by θ (c) S for a categorical latent c with P (c = k) = π k , where c is replicated over the index sets of the responses that depend on θ S or over a subset of them.

For the base, construct G with an rv vertex y annotated f (• | η), vertices for the parents z with dep edges into y, and par vertices (or edge labels) for β; W1, W2, and W6 hold, W3 to W5 are vacuous, and Equation 1 returns f (y | η).

Assume the claim for the components of each closure rule and construct: (composition) the union of the two diagrams on shared vertices, acyclic by hypothesis, so W1 holds, with W5 preserved because shared quantities carry the same plate membership in both components, and the product of the two factorizations is the joint; (Gaussian block) add cov edges between the responses in the specified positions, so W3 holds and the block density is the Gaussian with the marked free covariances; (replication) enclose the replicated substructure in a plate (S, I) whose nesting or crossing mirrors the index structure; every edge from an unreplicated quantity into the plate satisfies W5c because the plates of the tail are a subset of the plates of the head, and Equation 1 multiplies the component density over the copies; (mixing) add a lat, cat, rv vertex c inside the plates over which it is replicated, annotated with the categorical distribution π, a par vertex for π feeding c, and mix edges from c to the par vertices in S (or to the annotations that carry θ S ), so W4 holds and W5c holds because every response depending on θ S lies in the plates of c; the sum over the copies of c in Equation 2returns, for each copy ι of the replicated unit, k π k L ι,k (θ), and for an unreplicated c the whole-sample mixture k π k L k (θ).

text.text: Each construction preserves W1 to W6 and the identity between the induced family and the model, so by induction on the number of rule applications every member of M admits a well-formed UMG whose induced family is the model.
Result 3 (Path/RAM reduction).
Restrict to UMGs with one person plate, continuous random vertices, linear-Gaussian annotations, the statistical badge, and parameters drawn only as edge labels.

Forgetting the fill and role typing and drawing observed vertices as rectangles and latent vertices as ellipses is a bijection onto recursive Reticular Action Model path diagrams for covariance structures whose covariance-linked sets satisfy W3: the directed edges collect into the asymmetric matrix, the covariance edges and variances into the symmetric matrix, and the fill rule into the filter that selects observed variables (McArdle & McDonald, 1984; Bollen, 1989).

text.text: Result 4 (Plate/PGM reduction).
Restrict to UMGs without covariance edges in which every parameter has been given a prior.

Forgetting the role dimension leaves fill and shape, which is the plate notation of Bayesian graphical modeling (Buntine, 1994; Koller & Friedman, 2009; Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013), to which the directed Markov property and d-separation apply (Lauritzen et al., 1990).

text.text: Result 5 (Causal reduction).

Under the structural badge, the subgraph of stochastic edges among substantive vertices, after each covariance edge is replaced by a latent common cause, is a causal directed acyclic graph in the sense of Pearl (2009), and the do-calculus applies to it.
text.formatted: Under the structural badge, the subgraph of stochastic edges among substantive vertices, after each covariance edge is replaced by a latent common cause, is a causal directed acyclic graph in the sense of <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Pearl (2009)</ref>, and the do-calculus applies to it.

text.text: Under the statistical badge no interventional claim is licensed, whatever the direction of the edges.
Proof of Result 3.

Under the restriction, every vertex is continuous and random, the directed graph is acyclic by W1 so the model is recursive, the single plate contributes a product over persons of identical factors, and every annotation is linear-Gaussian with parameters on the edges; the mean structure, which the Reticular Action Model carries with a unit constant, extends the argument with a const vertex and is omitted here.

Write A for the matrix whose (i, j) entry is the label of the dep edge from j to i (zero if absent), S for the symmetric matrix whose off-diagonal entries are the labels of cov edges and whose diagonal entries are the variance annotations, and F for the selection matrix of observed vertices, read from fill.

Equation 1 then states that the vector of all vertices ν satisfies ν = Aν + ζ with Cov(ζ) = S, so the observed covariance is F (I -A) -1 S(I -A) -⊤ F ⊤ , which is the Reticular Action Model (McArdle & McDonald, 1984).
text.formatted: Equation 1 then states that the vector of all vertices ν satisfies ν = Aν + ζ with Cov(ζ) = S, so the observed covariance is F (I -A) -1 S(I -A) -⊤ F ⊤ , which is the Reticular Action Model <ref type="bibr">(McArdle & McDonald, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely any recursive RAM triple (A, S, F ) whose covariancelinked sets satisfy the merged-graph clause of W3 defines the edges, variances, and fills of a restricted UMG.
The two maps are inverse on this class, hence a bijection.
Proof of Result 4.

Without cov edges every block is a single vertex, and with every parameter given a prior every non-constant vertex has role rv or det; a parameter that carries a prior and is targeted by a mix edge becomes K random vertices in a plate over k, on which each child depends together with c, and a deterministic vertex is a degenerate conditional.

Forgetting role leaves fill (observed versus latent) and shape (continuous circles, categorical squares), which is the plate notation of Bayesian graphical modeling; the instantiated graph is a directed acyclic graph over random variables in which each vertex carries a conditional density given its parents, a Bayesian network with plates (Buntine, 1994; Koller & Friedman, 2009), and the directed Markov property and hence d-separation follow from the factorization (Lauritzen et al., 1990).

The UMG therefore comes with six well-formedness conditions, W1 to W6.

Two further design choices serve reproducible practice.

First, the package core imports only base R packages; lavaan, lme4, and the other modeling packages are suggested dependencies, loaded only when a converter is called, so the diagram machinery itself carries no modeling dependencies.

Second, a diagram is generated from a plain-text specification, so it belongs in a replication package the same way analysis code does: the specification can be versioned, diffed against a preregistered predecessor, and recompiled by a reader.

The occasion plate nests inside the person plate.

Y = yes; P = partial; N = no. O1 = build from a fitted model object; O2 = build from a specification without fitting; O3 = emit estimation syntax from the diagram object; O4 = validate well-formedness (refuse a non-model); O5 = scaling or identification check from the diagram; O6 = parameter count and degrees of freedom from the diagram; O7 = d-separation or implied conditional independencies; O8 = data displays generated from the model structure; O9 = vector or TikZ output; O10 = ggplot2 or Graphviz rendering backend. Protocol, scripts, and renderings: the benchmark materials in the OSF repository. The existing tools do their intended jobs well. The structural equation packages render a fitted lavaan or OpenMx model cleanly, with observed and latent nodes distinguished, covariance edges distinct from directed ones, and residuals shown. Several emit model syntax (semPlot, umx, dagitty, ggdag). The causal-graph packages derive d-separation statements and adjustment sets from a specification (dagitty, ggdag). tidySEM plots growth trajectories from a fitted mixture. None of them, however, represents the distinctions that Figure 1 turns on. No package draws a latent categorical variable as its own kind of object; tidySEM's rendering of a fitted two-class growth mixture failed outright, and umx's plot of the same mixture silently drew one class.
